prompt: A DDS oscillator uses a 32-bit unsigned phase register but only its high bits to index a waveform table. What is the role of the remaining low bits?

options.text: They retain progress between table entries, allowing finer frequency steps than the table index alone
options.explanation: Correct. The full phase register advances even when several successive updates select the same table entry.

options.text: They are unused, so clearing them after every sample cannot affect tuning
options.explanation: Clearing them loses fractional progress in table-index units and changes the oscillator’s timing.

options.text: They automatically remove all aliasing from the table
options.explanation: Phase precision does not constrain the table’s spectrum or eliminate interpolation errors.

options.text: They prevent the unsigned register from wrapping
options.explanation: The register still wraps over its full unsigned range; wrapping is the intended cycle boundary.

workedExample: Think of the full register as a precise cycle position and the high bits as a coarser viewing window. Low bits accumulate progress that eventually advances the visible table index. More phase precision gives a finer tuning grid; it does not enlarge the table or guarantee spectral quality.
